bibliography.abstract: The authors have previously demonstrated that students pursuing individual GIS projects adopted different strategies, recognising that further research was required to understand how they used online sources of help. Here, we explore how students engaged with these sources and provide future students with advice on how to use them more effectively and efficiently. Adopting self-efficacy as a theoretical construct, we analyse the students’ progress and the effects of their GIS projects on their self-confidence and resilience. We adopt a mixed-methods approach comprising two linked, online surveys, conducted before and after the project work, and a series of one-to-one, semi-structured interviews. The former sought to quantify confidence in using online sources of help and translating real-world problems into GIS. The latter sought to gain deeper insights into students’ resilience, given the challenges of GIS. We show that most students are significantly more confident after completing their GIS projects, supported by online sources of help, but for individuals, the areas and degrees of improvement are highly variable. We recommend that students develop a positive mindset when engaging with online sources of help and conclude that self-efficacy must be treated more critically to be considered operationally useful and theoretically insightful.

bibliography.title: Using individual GIS projects to build students’ self-efficacy: an empirical and theoretical study

publication_status.journal: Journal of Geography in Higher Education

en.caveats: The study relies on self-reported survey and interview data from a specific, unspecified student cohort rather than objective performance metrics.
en.what: This study evaluates how individual GIS projects affect student self-confidence and resilience using a mixed-methods approach. The researchers conducted two linked online surveys before and after the projects alongside a series of one-to-one, semi-structured interviews to measure confidence in translating real-world problems into GIS and utilizing online help. The findings show that while most students experienced a significant increase in confidence after completing their projects, the specific areas and degrees of improvement varied widely among individuals.
en.why: It demonstrates that independent project-based learning combined with online troubleshooting resources builds student resilience, while cautioning educators that self-efficacy gains are highly individualized rather than uniform.
